newsitem.title: USA: Weekly jobless claims up in latest week.
newsitem.headline: Weekly jobless claims up in latest week.

text.p: The number of Americans filing for first-time jobless benefits rose last week, the government said Thursday.

Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia said manufacturing jobs are continuing to grow moderately in the third U.S. economic district, which includes parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware.
The Labour Department said weekly jobless claims rose to 347,000 in the week ended June 14. Claims stood at 339,000 the week before.
Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters had expected 333,000 new claims. The level of claims last week was the highest since the week ended May 3, the department said.
The four-week moving average of claims, seen as a more reliable indicator of jobless trends than the more-volatile weekly figure, jumped to 335,500 from 329,250 the previous week.

A total of 2,295,000 people continued to file claims for unemployment benefits in the week ended June 7, the latest period for which the data were available, the department said. That was up from a revised 2,274,000 the week before.
The Philadelphia Fed's business outlook survey for the month of June showed that the business activity index jumped sharply, to 25.2 in June against a 1.6 reading in May.
"We continue some moderate growth in manufacturing employment in our district," said Michael Trebing, regional economist at the Philadelphia Fed.
Trebing also said he sees some continued underlying strength in regional demand. "On balance what (the numbers) are saying is that there is still underlying strength in demand and output," he said.

The Philadelphia Fed's report contrasted with a U.S. Federal Reserve report Wednesday that said the economy kept growing in May and early June, but there were "pockets of weakness." It said there were signs of a slowdown in several regions and that only scattered wage or price pressures were evident.

Analysts said the Fed's so-called Beige Book summary was the clearest sign yet that the central bank will not raise interest rates next month. The report reinforced the growing view that the central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee will hold rates steady at its July 1-2 meeting.
